Read /Documents/smooth-poincare-4d/papers/investigations-1/01_chiral_metric_evolution/continuation-notes/BROAD_RESEARCH_CONTINUATION_20261122.md\
and execute its “Pasteable prompt” as my instructions for this research run.\
\
I authorize the broad continuation and Sol 6.2 delegation described there.\
Begin now, preserving my selected lead model and effort.\

I’ll read the continuation prompt and required project records, then begin the authorized research run. I’ll preserve the lead settings and use bounded Sol 6.2 delegation where the workflow permits it.

The register confirms that the foundation audit has not yet run. I’ll start there, with fixed audit work delegated to Sol 6.2, while I examine Fine’s nonlinear flow and the real sphere-bundle formulation. I also verified this chat’s identity and found its local source for public-text capture.

The audit’s first return supports the manuscript’s internal flow normalization, but flags a possible mismatch with Fine’s printed norm and time conventions. I’ll resolve that before citing a time conversion. The nonlinear calculation will keep the manuscript’s explicit equation and separate direction distortion from horizontal transport and metric scale.

The remaining audit returns support the TT factor-four comparison, the fourth-order metric-gradient distinction, and the boundary example within their stated scopes. I’m checking the twistor inputs next; I’ll use the PDF skill to inspect the AHS theorem so the real-coordinate formulation rests on its actual hypotheses.

The twistor sources identify a key distinction for the coordinate method: complete sphere fibers support fiberwise complex geometry, but the earlier reconstruction also assumes holomorphic transport. The next comparison will therefore track the horizontal mismatch \(A-\Gamma_A^+\) and the \(W^+\) obstruction explicitly, rather than infer their control from two-patch coordinates.

The first nonlinear calculation has produced a useful candidate result: Fine’s unadjusted flow appears to preserve the curvature volume form pointwise, beyond conserving total volume. I’m having that checked independently. The principal equation also contains coupling between eigenvalues that prevents a straightforward scalar minimum-eigenvalue argument; we still need to determine what that means for actual connection data.

The independent check confirms pointwise volume preservation. It also constructs smooth local definite connection data where the smallest eigenvalue initially decreases at a strict spatial minimum. That rules out a naive monotonicity claim in this local setting; it does not show loss of definiteness along a solution.

I’m now testing a whole-fiber transport remainder that measures the horizontal derivatives appearing in the nonlinear equation, with the round two-patch first-jet construction as its calibration.

The whole-fiber calculation now gives a precise reconstruction identity: its nonholomorphic transport remainder measures horizontal strain and controls both \(\nabla_AQ\) and \(A-\Gamma_A^+\), without assuming an eigenvalue floor.

I’ve split the next work into two checks: whether a bound on that remainder would preserve definiteness, and whether the exact nonlinear equation gives energy decay while the defect remains uniformly small. Both still require hypotheses that the flow has not been shown to preserve.

The new calculations give a conditional route from control of the fibre transport error to curvature pinching and energy decay. I’m checking the constants and hypotheses before integrating them; the main missing step is still an estimate that keeps that transport error controlled along the flow.

Two shortcuts now fail in explicit examples: affine averaging can destroy definiteness even between gauge-equivalent round connections, and zero flow speed at a point can coexist with large horizontal strain there. I’m testing what stronger spatial estimates could bridge that gap, while keeping those local examples separate from claims about singularities or global flow.

There is now a stronger geometric estimate: the horizontal strain and its first derivative control \(W^+\), traceless Ricci curvature and scalar curvature, with constants that do not require an assumed lower eigenvalue bound for \(Q\). This makes the coordinate approach more concrete. It still needs an evolution estimate for those derivatives, and the opposite Weyl component requires a separate argument.

The concentration tests show that small defect energy, small squared flow speed, and even a small spatial \(L^4\) strain norm do not by themselves control the worst distortion. I’m now checking a time-dependent criterion: whether integrating the supremum of the strain derivative and squared strain controls both the metric and definiteness. That would state a concrete missing estimate for the flow.

The temporal criterion checks out: a finite time integral of \(\sup(|\nabla^A T|+|T|^2)\) keeps the metric comparable to its initial metric and keeps \(Q\) quantitatively positive. The strain equation also has the same self-adjoint diffusion coefficient as the \(Q\) equation. I’m testing its energy estimate next and checking the integrated manuscript.

The strain-energy calculation now gives a useful conditional result: with a sufficiently small pointwise \(Q\)-defect and a uniform Sobolev bound along the interval, initially small \(L^4\) strain remains small and decays. The remaining gaps are proving those geometric hypotheses persist and obtaining the stronger derivative control needed for continuation. The manuscript audit has also caught notation and zero-case inequalities, which I’m correcting.

The endpoint estimate works in the flat heat model: the initial \(L^{4,1}\) strain norm controls the time integral required by the metric-distortion estimate. I’m checking its transfer to the round chiral bundle and recording which steps still depend on unproved control of the nonlinear geometry.

The flat semilinear model also closes for small \(L^{4,1}\) data, including quadratic derivative terms and cubic terms. Fine’s varying second-order operator remains a separate difficulty. I’m testing whether the direct forcing estimate needed to absorb that operator is valid; a failed estimate would tell us which analytic approach to avoid.

The gauge audit found a detail that needs verification: differentiating the metric-dependent adjoint in the printed gauge formula appears to introduce third derivatives away from the reference connection. I’m checking that calculation independently and testing a fixed-metric adjoint. This affects the continuation argument we can justify; it does not establish that Fine’s existence result is false.

The independent calculation confirms the derivative-order issue. Freezing the metric only in the vertical adjoint removes the third derivative and preserves the parabolic reference symbol. I’m now checking the local PDE theorem and the transformation back to the original flow. The manuscript also includes the endpoint estimates and the precise failure of the direct forcing argument.

The local fixed-adjoint construction now has both analytic pieces: a short-time solution theorem and a checked transformation back to the original flow. A separate possibility has emerged from the energy estimates: they may force a time slice that satisfies the known sphere theorem, without first proving convergence of the whole flow. I’m testing that conditional implication next.

The energy estimates give a conditional route to recognizing the smooth sphere: if the flow stays smooth and satisfies the stated pinching and Sobolev bounds for an explicit finite time, one time slice meets the known sphere theorem. I’m integrating that result and checking a possible route to the missing regularity estimates.

The curvature-symbol calculation is positive: adding a term that vanishes by the Bianchi identity gives a coercive symbol on all curvature components at a definite reference. A nonlinear system with a proved compatibility condition is still missing. In parallel, I’m checking whether a scalar-curvature identity can establish positive Yamabe constant from the strain itself, without a derivative bound.

The scalar identity checks out. With the stated Sobolev constant, sufficiently small critical \(L^4\) strain gives positive Yamabe constant, without small curvature defect or a quantitative eigenvalue floor. The coupled connection–curvature calculation also appears to preserve compatibility; I’m reviewing that derivation before using it for further regularity work.

The coupled system now checks at the smooth level: it is parabolic near a definite reference, and compatible data keep \(F=F_A\). I also found a relevant rough-data framework in Koch–Lamm. Its use here still needs a bundle-level argument and careful control of the gauge transformation, so it does not yet turn the continuous endpoint limits into smooth continuation.
Please make sure to keep track of references following the guidance in REFERENCE_WORKFLOW

I’ll check the reference records against `REFERENCE_WORKFLOW.md`, including exact versions, source locations, theorem dependencies and access limitations, then update any gaps while continuing the research.
Also, feel free to update the manuscript with new results as you go

I’m updating the working manuscript as results pass review. It now includes the fixed-adjoint local construction, the compatible connection–curvature system, the Yamabe bound and the finite-time conditional sphere criterion. I’ll keep the hypotheses explicit and rebuild and check the PDF after this integration pass.

The shared catalog and bibliography now include Koch–Lamm’s exact inspected preprint version. I also clarified Taylor’s undated, repaginated reading copy, added the recent theorem dependencies and recorded the existing Fine PDF’s size and hash. The records distinguish remote readings from retained files and keep the unavailable journal text marked as uninspected.

The manuscript builds cleanly. Its labels, references and bibliography order pass the checks, and all manuscript citations have entries in the shared bibliography. I’m checking the rendered pages while the next bounded analysis addresses the compact-bundle estimates needed for the rough-data construction.

The 59-page PDF is rebuilt and visually checked, including the new gauge, curvature-system and sphere-recognition sections. The next step is narrower than full continuation: testing whether the adjusted system admits solutions from small continuous connection–curvature data. Those linear and nonlinear arguments are still under review; I haven’t promoted them to manuscript results.

The linear estimate audit passed. The nonlinear audit has identified a detail to make explicit: the forcing terms must lie in a completion that gives a uniform initial trace. I’ll incorporate that detail before adding the rough local result to the manuscript, with the distinction between adjusted and original flow kept explicit.

The combined argument now supports a local result for the adjusted connection–curvature system: sufficiently small continuous data near one fixed smooth definite reference produce a solution that is smooth at positive times and preserves curvature compatibility. I’m adding it to the manuscript. A bounded follow-up is checking whether the same uniform lifespan gives continuation whenever an adjusted trajectory stays in that value neighborhood.

The continuation check passed in the adjusted gauge: staying in a sufficiently small value neighborhood of the same fixed reference rules out a finite smooth endpoint. The next question is whether small data remain controlled. I’m checking Fine’s near-perfect stability argument and a gauge with frozen reference operators, to see whether the new local smoothing result can connect to long-time stability.

The manuscript audit supports the new theorem and identified several proof steps to spell out. I’ve added the causal-kernel identity, the completed-space trace argument, and the uniqueness argument used to preserve compatibility. The source records now distinguish the inspected Koch–Lamm preprint and Taylor text from their publication metadata and identify where the manuscript uses them.

The 63-page manuscript has rebuilt cleanly, and the new section has passed visual review. The stability checks have also found two issues in the source’s displayed implementation: a third-order term in the live gauge and a mismatch between the stated initial-data space and its parabolic norm. The helpers are checking fixed-reference operators and a direct energy estimate; neither issue alone disproves the source’s stability conclusion.

The fixed-reference stability inputs are now checked: the round operator has a positive spectral gap, and the nonlinear remainder has the quadratic Sobolev bounds needed for a contraction argument. The nonlinear proof is underway. The transfer argument also checks out conditionally: positive-time smoothing would extend stability to smooth inputs small in connection and curvature values, without a bound on their higher derivatives.

The focused audits have returned without a blocking defect. I’m checking their final arguments before adding the near-round stability result to the manuscript. The reference records distinguish the source theorems we inspected from bibliography pointers we have not verified.

The manuscript now includes the stability proof and its consequence for the original flow: smooth connections sufficiently close to the round reference in both connection and curvature values evolve globally and converge modulo time-dependent bundle automorphisms. This is a result on the standard sphere; constructing suitable initial data on arbitrary homotopy four-spheres remains open. I’m auditing the manuscript wording and continuing the separate test of critical-norm control for the highest-order nonlinear terms.

The updated manuscript builds cleanly at 66 pages. The integration audit has identified a few wording fixes about which adjoints stay fixed and which remain live; the underlying stability argument is unchanged. The critical-norm calculation also checks out for the linear heat problem, and a helper is testing the specified quasilinear model next.

The quasilinear flat model now closes in the critical norm, including the highest-order coefficient perturbation and quadratic gradient terms. That is still a model result. Two follow-up tasks address the geometric application: transferring the linear estimate to a fixed compact bundle, and checking how the resulting path norm bounds the real sphere-bundle strain used in the temporal distortion criterion.

The stability checkpoint is now saved as a verified 67-page manuscript, with all audit corrections integrated. The compact-bundle critical estimate has also been derived, and the strain calculation shows precisely what it would control. The next check applies that estimate to the actual coupled geometric equation and proves that its critical-norm solution agrees with the already established smooth solution.

The actual coupled equation now has the requested local critical-norm estimate. Its proof also establishes agreement with the earlier adjusted solution for smooth compatible data, which preserves curvature compatibility. The focused audit is underway. Combined with the stable tail, this is the remaining input for a whole-time strain bound from the stronger initial norm.

The smoothing argument also gives a linear estimate at a fixed positive time. Together, the checked steps bound the total strain budget by the initial critical pair norm. I’m reviewing that combined implication and the reference records before adding it to the manuscript. A separate test now asks whether intrinsic strain controls the stronger norm under explicit gauge conditions; existence of such a gauge remains a separate question.

The cross-check supports a linear bound for total strain from the small critical connection–curvature norm. I’m integrating that result into the manuscript and correcting the reference records. The fixed-slice strain estimate has also returned; it will get an independent check before I use it.

The reference audit found no unresolved citation keys. I’m expanding Taylor’s recorded coverage to include the composition and commutator estimates used here, adding precise Fine formula citations, and linking the later consumers. The three unread rigidity references remain marked as pointers only.

The new manuscript section is being checked against the derivation notes while the PDF builds. I’ve also started the next slice calculation: the linear projection should separate the gauge directions, but a finite coordinate change introduces additional derivative terms. That distinction matters for any later claim based on intrinsic strain alone.

The fixed-slice estimate passed its second check: small live Lorentz strain controls the full critical pair norm, provided both slice equations already hold. I’m adding that conditional result. The new bounds also suggest that the recovering automorphisms may converge in \(C^1\); a separate packet is testing that consequence and its precise regularity.

The expanded draft builds cleanly, and all internal references and bibliography keys resolve. The manuscript checks retained the key restrictions: smooth compatible data, a fixed round reference, and an assumed slice for the intrinsic-strain corollary. I’m finishing the layout checks and reviewing the possible limiting-automorphism result separately.

The 74-page checkpoint is saved and visually checked. The next calculation asks whether the recovery converges smoothly at every derivative order. It uses decay in one fixed low norm to absorb the higher-order terms later in time, with constants allowed to depend on the smooth input.

The independent audit confirms smooth convergence in every fixed derivative order within the existing round small-value basin. I’m adding that result to the manuscript, including the limiting bundle automorphism and metric. The slice work has also identified a finite-dimensional residual that must be checked before claiming nonlinear slice existence.

The manuscript now includes the smooth-limit proof. Its smallness threshold is fixed at one low Sobolev order; estimates for higher derivatives follow later along the same solution. I’m checking the separate critical-norm bound on the limiting automorphism and auditing the slice inverse’s regularity claims.

The manuscript audit caught a precision issue: two constructions can choose different recovery automorphisms for the same original flow. I’ve corrected the quantitative claim to refer to its own construction. The source audit also found a possible nonlinear slice route through Hamilton’s local surjection theorem; its full smooth-tame hypotheses still need verification.

The 77-page manuscript checkpoint is saved, with clean build and layout checks. I’m now checking two prerequisites for a smooth local slice construction in parallel: smooth dependence of the elliptic inverse, and compatible charts for the bundle automorphism group. Even if both succeed, that would give a local smooth result, not slice placement throughout the value-small basin.

The elliptic solver now has a derived smooth-tame family estimate, so it is ready for independent review. I’m also checking the geometric consequence of a slice representative: the live Lorentz strain norm is preserved by bundle pullback, which could transfer the whole-time bound without controlling derivatives of the chosen automorphism.

The first independent checks support the local construction and its intrinsic-strain consequence. The precise claim is an open neighborhood in the smooth topology, including all its smooth bundle pullbacks. I’m preparing the manuscript statement with that hypothesis explicit; placement under connection and curvature value bounds alone remains unresolved.

The manuscript review supports the new local section and intrinsic-strain result. I’m incorporating its precision edits and checking the rebuilt PDF. The next calculation tests whether the infinitesimal slice solver has uniform Lorentz bounds under value smallness alone; that would address part of the remaining placement problem.

The updated manuscript builds cleanly at 80 pages. It states the intrinsic-strain result on a smooth neighborhood of the round orbit and leaves extension to the full value-small basin open. The endpoint solver calculation has also returned a positive result; I’ll check its uniform constants before using it.

The endpoint calculation uses only uniform bounds on the connection and curvature differences; its independent audit is nearly complete. I’m also checking what the intrinsic budget implies for the initial metric, and testing a periodic model to see whether the horizontal solver can have a uniform \(C^1\) bound under critical smallness.

The geometric consequence is precise: within the assessed neighborhood, small intrinsic strain makes the initial metric uniformly close to a round pullback, with exactly the same volume form. The periodic test also shows that critical smallness cannot give a uniform instantaneous \(C^1\) bound for the frozen horizontal solver. I’m checking its finite flow separately before drawing any conclusion about slice placement.

The derivative example now extends to actual pullbacks of the round chiral connection, and its audit is underway. The input pairs approach the reference in the critical norm while this solver’s horizontal \(C^1\) output grows. Its auxiliary finite flows still converge in \(C^1\). This narrows the failed estimate without ruling out finite slice placement.

Both checks for the internal gauge step have returned positive preliminary results: a finite Coulomb gauge from small Lorentz data, and a derivative bound once that representative is supplied. The first proof includes the required smoothness argument. I’m reviewing them while finishing the manuscript checks; the horizontal slice equation remains separate.

The manuscript audit found no substantive correction to the curved example. Its small wording fixes are in place. I’m now arranging a separate audit of the finite Coulomb gauge and its regularity estimate before combining them into a new result.

The new gauge calculation gives a useful intermediate estimate: small connection and curvature values yield a Coulomb representative with a controlled derivative norm. I’m also testing whether Lorentz strain directly bounds the pointwise defect \(Q-I\); that would give pinching without first solving the horizontal slice equation.

The 83-page manuscript is now built, checked and saved to the normal PDF location. The latest static calculation also gives a preliminary strain-to-pinching estimate without either slice equation. Separately, the existing global value basin may supply the interval assumptions needed by the earlier strain-energy estimates; I’m checking that implication next.

The checks now distinguish two effects. Lorentz strain controls the pointwise defect, while a zero-strain example retains large critical curvature oscillations after internal Coulomb gauge fixing. The global energy check has also found that the earlier \(L^2\) and \(L^4\) decay estimates apply throughout the existing small-value basin, once initial \(L^4\) strain is sufficiently small.

The independent reviews passed both static results and the global energy consequence. I’m adding them to the manuscript with their scope stated explicitly: pinching and integrated strain decay are established in the stated round basin; the stronger supremum-in-time budget still needs an argument. A multiscale heat-model test is examining that remaining distinction.

The global energy result passed review, with a few wording changes needed to make its smallness assumptions explicit. The new multiscale calculation also extends to the actual round linearized flow. I’m sending that extension for independent review and checking what it implies for the nonlinear estimate.

The example separates the remaining estimates more sharply: small initial \(L^4\) strain does not control the linearized time integral of the supremum of its derivative. I’m checking whether this rules out the corresponding uniform linear bound for the nonlinear flow, and whether the stronger \(L^{4,1}\) norm accounts for the accumulated scales. These are separate claims from nonlinear blowup.

The manuscript’s 91-page checkpoint now includes the finite internal gauge, static defect estimate, and global strain-energy decay. It compiles cleanly, and I’ve checked the changed pages and new proofs visually. I’ve also updated the canonical reference record with the exact Ludewig theorem passages used for the round heat-kernel calculation.

The Lorentz calculation identifies the expected threshold: for this family, \(L^{4,1}\) counts all the scales contributing to the derivative integral, and the earlier round heat estimate gives a matching upper bound. Larger Lorentz indices lose that control. The nonlinear \(L^4\) derivative test has also returned; I’m auditing it before integrating the conclusion.

The next test addresses a stronger question: whether the nonlinear error can be controlled uniformly over all the shrinking time windows. The proposed proof uses the existing rough-solution spaces at each parabolic scale. If it survives audit, it could transfer the growing budget to smooth nonlinear solutions; the current fixed-window argument alone does not establish that.

The multiscale and finite-window results have passed their manuscript review. I’ve clarified the fixed-round scope and the order of limits in the draft. The uniform nonlinear remainder is now under a separate proof audit; the reference check confirms that this bound must be established in our compact-bundle setting, rather than imported directly from the scalar rough-data theorem.

The scale-uniform remainder audit passed. It supports the next step: testing whether actual nonlinear flows can have arbitrarily large accumulated strain even as their initial curvature strain tends to zero. The transfer derivation is ready for an independent check. The manuscript and PDF are also updated through the preceding results, at 95 pages.

The nonlinear transfer check has found no gap so far: it gives a family of smooth global flows whose initial values and \(L^4\) strain tend to zero while their finite accumulated budgets grow without bound. I’m integrating the proof after the written audit is complete. This leaves the stronger \(L^{4,1}\) endpoint open across the full value-small basin, so I’m next examining the exact defect equation that an endpoint estimate would need.

The nonlinear result has passed its written audit and is now in the working manuscript, with the uniform remainder proof included. The next calculation is promising but still under review: in the normalized defect \(Q\), the highest derivatives of the coordinate correction appear to cancel against the changing volume. I’m checking that cancellation before using it in an endpoint estimate.

The equation check confirms the cancellation: after normalization, only first derivatives of the background pair remain outside the principal defect Hessian. A separate estimate is testing whether those coefficients can be controlled by their short-time smoothing bounds. If it holds, it may give an \(L^{4,1}\) budget estimate on a fixed initial time interval; the later-time estimate would still need its own proof.

The manuscript now has a verified 100-page PDF, including the nonlinear family result and its full proof. I checked every changed page and kept the two new theorem statements together across page breaks. The \(L^{4,1}\) investigation is continuing in separate notes: the initial-interval argument has closed conditionally, and the uniform later-time estimate is still being worked through.

The independent check of the initial-interval estimate has found no gap: sufficiently small connection and curvature values give a bound proportional to the initial \(L^{4,1}\) strain, without a separate smallness condition on that strain norm. The remaining step is to make the later-time bound proportional to the same quantity, with constants independent of higher initial derivatives.

The initial-interval estimate is now assessed. The later-time argument has returned and is ready for an independent check, especially of whether its constants are independent of higher initial derivatives. Together, these would give the endpoint bound throughout the small connection-and-curvature basin.

The proposed bound also gives a quantitative comparison with one round bundle pullback, using the same limiting map for the connection, curvature and metric. I’m checking that consequence separately and preparing the manuscript proofs, with each estimate tied to its assessed inputs and reference record.

The independent tail check has found no gap so far. Its key estimate preserves the initial defect size through smoothing and exponential decay, so the bound appears to be \(C\ell\), with no separate smallness condition on \(\ell=\|T_{\mathrm{in}}\|_{L^{4,1}}\). This is still a result within the round value basin.

The whole-time \(L^{4,1}\) estimate and the comparison with one round limit are now assessed. I’m integrating them into the manuscript. In parallel, the next calculation applies the estimate to the real direction-sphere construction, testing time-integrated control of its horizontal comparison and the reconstructed positive chiral curvature.

The manuscript builds to 107 pages. The new section is under review; the first pass has flagged wording that needs clearer scope and one oversized display. Reference keys and cross-references pass the static checks, and the earlier round-defect section is unchanged.

The manuscript audit passed, and I’ve applied its clarifications. I’m also testing a separate continuation question: whether finite accumulated strain prevents a finite-time breakdown for general definite data. The key dependency is a local existence theorem whose allowed value radius is independent of reference derivatives; that refinement is still being checked.

The 107-page manuscript is now verified, and the normal PDF output has been updated. The real direction-sphere calculation has also passed its preliminary independent check, including the horizontal derivative and time-integrated positive chiral curvature bound. The general finite-time continuation argument remains conditional on the local-theory refinement.

The two new arguments are ready for review: a local existence radius uniform over bounded positive curvature data, and a restart argument using finite accumulated strain. I’m assigning separate audits before treating their combination as a general continuation theorem. The manuscript’s real-twistor comparison passed review with two local clarifications to apply.

Both continuation audits have found no gap so far. The key step is to choose one smooth reference before selecting a late smooth slice; its local existence time can then carry that slice past the proposed endpoint. This avoids needing uniform derivative bounds for the recovery maps. I’m also rebuilding the manuscript and updating the reference records.

The verified manuscript is now 110 pages, including the real direction-sphere estimates. The general restart argument has passed its conditional audit; the uniform-radius audit is finishing. I’m next checking whether the sphere-bundle transport remainder gives an equivalent form of the continuation quantity, with no near-round assumption.

The combined continuation theorem has now passed assessment: finite accumulated strain at a finite endpoint implies smooth extension of the original flow in the chosen definite component, without a near-round or small-budget assumption. I’ve added its proof to the manuscript for an integration audit. Proving that general initial data keep this budget finite remains open.

The reference audit passed. I’ve corrected stale catalog wording and linked the newer results to the exact source versions and passages already checked, preserving their inspection status. The new general-continuation proof builds cleanly; its integration audit is checking the proof’s abbreviated steps before the next PDF checkpoint.

The real sphere-bundle remainder now gives an equivalent continuation criterion, with explicit constants that remain valid across the full positive definite cone. The next audit is checking a compactness formulation: whether one positive uniform limit of normalized connection/curvature slices suffices for continuation. A bounded literature search is also distinguishing comparable results for other flows from results about this exact equation.

The sequential criterion passed review: one positive uniform limit of normalized connection/curvature slices suffices for smooth continuation, without uniform derivative bounds on the normalization maps. The literature search found a related extension theorem for the hypersymplectic flow, but its equation and hypotheses differ. I’ve recorded that distinction; the limited search does not establish novelty.

The manuscript audit passed both continuation corollaries and identified a few wording fixes. I’m applying those and rebuilding the PDF. A helper is also checking whether the scalar estimate used for the related hypersymplectic flow can apply to this equation, with the conclusion confined to the local calculation.

The updated manuscript builds cleanly at 117 pages; I’m checking the rendered pages before replacing the verified PDF. The exact scalar calculation also shows why the related flow’s trace maximum argument does not transfer directly. That finding is local—it does not establish a singular solution or failure of a global bound.

The new continuation proofs pass the layout check. I’m recording the 117-page checkpoint and updating the reference links. Next I’m testing whether explicit bounds on a sequence of geometries can supply the compactness required by the continuation criterion; the exact metric compactness theorem is being checked first.

The determinant-normalized trace test passed its audit: it rules out the proposed local scalar maximum argument, but says nothing by itself about global breakdown. For the compactness route, Anderson’s author survey provides the required metric theorem on a fixed closed manifold. I’m checking the separate step that lifts metric convergence to connection and curvature convergence.

A promising refinement is under review for homotopy four-spheres. The proposed argument uses topology to exclude a degenerate curvature limit once metric compactness and strain bounds are supplied. It would remove one extra hypothesis from the compactness criterion, but it still would not produce those bounds along the flow.

The topology audit passed: with a positive metric limit and the stated strain bounds, a homotopy four-sphere cannot develop a degenerate curvature matrix in that limit. I’m integrating this conditional result into the manuscript. The source review leaves injectivity radius as a separate required bound; the available compactness results do not yet remove it.

The manuscript will now state a more specific continuation criterion: along one sequence approaching a finite endpoint, bounded real transport density, a positive injectivity radius bound and a diameter bound suffice on a homotopy four-sphere. I’m also checking two remaining dependencies separately: which ALE ends can embed in that topology, and which compactness theorem supplies the required smooth ALE limit.

The manuscript additions are written and undergoing an independent integration audit. The reference check found a relevant correction to Bando’s bubbling paper; it is being recorded with the original source. That paper treats Einstein sequences, so its extraction theorem cannot yet be used for our weaker bounded-Ricci hypotheses.

The integration audit found notation issues to correct, including distinguishing the spatial derivative of \(f(Q(x))\) from the matrix derivative of \(f\). The underlying estimates still match the assessed derivations. A separate topology calculation also looks promising: the remaining smooth ALE quotient ends appear incompatible with an embedded core in an integral homology four-sphere, provided such a core is actually obtained from the metrics.

The current manuscript builds cleanly at 121 pages; I’m applying the audit’s final clarifications and checking the rendered pages. The literature check has located the Ricci-flat ALE theorem needed by the next proposed route. The remaining proof task is to obtain a smooth, nonflat limit with those hypotheses without assuming injectivity radius.

The 120-page manuscript checkpoint is now verified and saved, with the contents layout corrected. The proposed metric-limit argument is written and ready for an independent proof audit. If it passes, it may remove the injectivity assumption from the continuation criterion; I’m keeping that improvement out of the manuscript until the analytic argument is assessed.

The independent audit has passed the minimum harmonic-radius argument, including the compact embeddings and the proof that the limit is nonflat. I’m now checking how it combines with the ALE classification and updating the reference records before using the stronger conclusion in the manuscript.

The source check supports the needed ALE theorem without an extra decay or injectivity assumption. I also found inconsistent page locators in the Anderson reference notes; I’m checking the actual PDF pages so the canonical record can distinguish the original compactness theorem from the argument developed here.

The proposed stronger criterion now has a complete proof draft: on a supplied homotopy-sphere flow, bounds on the real transport quantity \(\Psi\) and diameter along one late sequence would suffice for continuation. A separate audit is checking the remaining global compactness step. The earlier manuscript checkpoint still states the assessed criterion while that audit runs.

The compactness audit is complete, and I’ve assessed the stronger continuation criterion: \(\Psi\) and diameter bounds on one late sequence suffice on a homotopy four-sphere. I’m integrating the proof into the manuscript. In parallel, a new bounded calculation tests whether sufficiently small intrinsic strain itself forces curvature pinching and positive Ricci curvature.

The manuscript now builds cleanly at 126 pages; its new proof is undergoing a final integration audit. The small-strain calculation also closes at the single-slice level: it excludes the nearly rank-one curvature alternative and yields positive Ricci curvature. That result is being independently checked before I use it to test entry into the established round-flow stability regime.

The small-strain result has passed its independent audit. Its key point is topological: the nearly rank-one case would produce a closed two-form with strictly positive square, which is impossible on this base. I’m adding that result and checking the separate step from small initial strain to global convergence of the actual flow.

The audit of positive-time round entry has passed. A broader result is also ready for review: with bounded initial strain and diameter, sufficiently small total defect energy leads to global convergence. I’m checking that extension and the manuscript’s revised pages before updating the saved PDF.

The revised compactness section removes the need for a separate injectivity-radius bound on a homotopy four-sphere. Its use of the ALE classification is now tied to the exact inspected source passages. The next argument uses energy dissipation to obtain a smooth perfect connection at positive time, then applies the established round stability result to the original flow.

I’m integrating the intrinsic entry theorem and tightening the abstract around the main results. The next calculation asks what bounded geometry along a sequence of late slices implies when the energy does not tend to zero. It may produce a critical limiting connection; whether that connection must be perfect is a separate question.

The energy-entry theorem has passed its proof audit. The manuscript review found wording to clarify, including the norm used for “small intrinsic strain” and the distinction between the cited signature theorem and our curvature-normalization calculation. The late-sequence argument also checks so far: positive limiting energy yields a critical accumulation point, while zero limiting energy yields convergence to a fixed round pullback.

The late-sequence result has now passed audit.
